title: Egyrészt... Másrészt...: Weighing Advantages and Disadvantages

sections.title: Laying two sides on the table
sections.content: When you're helping someone weigh a choice, *egyrészt* ("on one hand") ... *másrészt* ("on the other hand") lays out an *előny* (advantage) and a *hátrány* (disadvantage) side by side, evenhandedly, before either of you commits to a preference. It's more structured than a plain *de* ("but") — it signals from the very first word that a second, contrasting point is coming.

items.spanish: Egyrészt olcsóbb a vonat, másrészt tovább tart az út.
items.english: On one hand the train is cheaper; on the other hand, the trip takes longer.

items.spanish: Ennek a munkának egyrészt sok előnye van, másrészt komoly hátrányai is.
items.english: This job has a lot of advantages on one hand, but also serious disadvantages on the other.

items.spanish: Egyrészt szeretnék elköltözni, másrészt félek a változástól.
items.english: On one hand I'd like to move, on the other hand I'm afraid of the change.

sections.content: *egyrészt* and *másrészt* always come as a pair, each opening its own clause. Using *másrészt* on its own, without an *egyrészt* earlier in the conversation, sounds like you've skipped the first half of your own thought.
